---
title: "Predicting observations the model did not see"
---

Suppose a regression predicts reading time from word length, frequency, and contextual predictability. Small residuals show that its fitted values are close to the responses used to estimate the coefficients. They do not tell us how the fitted procedure will predict a response that was unavailable during fitting.

The phrase *unavailable during fitting* must be made precise. A reading-time dataset may contain repeated responses from readers and passages. We could omit one response while retaining other responses from the same reader and passage, omit every response from one reader, or omit every word position in one passage. Each split evaluates a different prediction.

| predictive question | omitted during fitting | represented prediction |
|:--|:--|:--|
| another trial | one response | another response from observed readers and passages |
| a new reader | every response from one reader | responses from a reader absent during fitting |
| a new passage | every position in one passage | responses from a passage absent during fitting |

A random split over rows can evaluate the first question. It cannot evaluate prediction for a new reader or passage because other rows from that reader or passage remain available during fitting.

## Defining the predictive comparison

[What must be new at prediction time](prediction-targets.qmd) identifies which observations or groups must be absent during fitting and what information will be available about them. A [predictive loss](predictive-loss.qmd) assigns a numerical cost to each difference between an observation and its prediction. The aggregation of those losses determines whether readers, passages, or individual rows receive equal weight.

[Training and test data](training-and-test-data.qmd) separate fitting from evaluation. [Cross-validation](cross-validation.qmd) repeats that separation so that each observation receives a prediction from a fit that did not use it. [Leave-one-out cross-validation](leave-one-out-cross-validation.qmd) omits one observation at a time, while [grouped cross-validation](grouped-cross-validation.qmd) omits complete speakers, items, passages, or languages.

## Comparing models

Predictive comparison can test a linguistic contrast. A control model might contain design and lexical predictors, while a second model adds a measure of syntactic predictability. [Comparing predictive loss](comparing-predictive-loss.qmd) asks whether the added predictor changes loss on the same held-out observations. The coefficient for syntactic predictability and the change in held-out loss are related, but they are not the same quantity.

[Likelihood-ratio tests](likelihood-ratio-tests.qmd) and [information criteria](information-criteria.qmd) make different comparisons using the fitted likelihood. [PSIS-LOO](psis-loo.qmd) approximates leave-one-out prediction from posterior draws, while [WAIC](waic.qmd) uses a posterior-variance correction to the pointwise fitted predictive density.

[PS2](../assignments/index.qmd) applies grouped cross-validation to reading-time data by withholding complete passages. The passage split, passage-level loss summaries, and interpretation all follow from the target of predicting responses in passages absent during fitting.
